Learning objectives

  • Identify normal bone regions, lamellar versus woven bone, osteoblasts and osteoclasts.
  • Classify major primary bone tumors using the lecture’s WHO 2020 framework and recognize the major clinical pointers.
  • Differentiate osteoid osteoma and osteosarcoma.
  • Differentiate osteochondroma, enchondroma and chondrosarcoma.
  • Explain fibrous dysplasia, giant cell tumor, and Ewing sarcoma by clinicopathologic presentation and outcome.

Big picture

Patient age + bone compartment + location + matrix + growth behavior + histology identifies a bone lesion. Osteoid, cartilage, fibrous tissue, osteoclast-like giant cells, and small round blue cells form different patterns. When you can move between these observations, the tumors are easier to distinguish than by memorizing eight separate lists.

1 · Bone anatomy, histology & tumor biology

The bone compartment and matrix identify what kind of tissue is involved. Epiphysis is the articular end, metaphysis is adjacent to the growth plate, and diaphysis is the shaft. Long bone location is one of the quickest ways to narrow a bone-tumor differential.

Normal lamellar bone has organized collagen layers and mature structural strength; woven bone is immature, disorganized bone. Cortical and trabecular lamellar bone appear differently under the microscope. Osteoblasts deposit bone matrix; multinucleated osteoclasts resorb bone in Howship lacunae.

FOUNDATIONS LINK
Bone remodeling requires coordination of bone-forming osteoblasts and bone-resorbing osteoclasts. Tumor morphology and osteolysis become easier to understand once these normal roles are clear.
A lesion is centered in the epiphysis of a skeletally mature patient. Which tumor should move up your differential?
Giant cell tumor of bone; the location becomes especially characteristic after physeal closure.

2 · Classification, clinical presentation & first imaging

The lecture uses WHO 2020 categories: benign, intermediate (locally aggressive, sometimes rarely metastasizing), and malignant. Osteogenic tumors make osteoid/bone; chondrogenic tumors make cartilage; Ewing is an undifferentiated round-cell sarcoma; giant cell tumor belongs to osteoclastic giant cell-rich tumors.

MUST KNOW
The lecture emphasizes that metastatic lesions are much more common than primary bone malignancies, especially over age 40. Its “most common primary malignant” ranking refers to non-hematopoietic primary bone tumors; hematopoietic malignancies are classified separately.

Common benign lesions are frequently incidental, or produce intermittent activity-related pain; malignant lesions more often cause progressive pain at rest/night, a growing mass, functional loss, or fracture. Osteoid osteoma is the important benign exception: nocturnal pain relieved by NSAIDs.

Start with a plain radiograph and consider age, bone, and exact longitudinal location. Enneking’s four questions: (1) where is the lesion, (2) what is the tumor doing to bone, (3) how is the bone reacting, (4) what is the matrix?

Why does age over 40 fundamentally change the differential for an aggressive bone lesion?
Metastatic bone disease and hematologic malignancies rise in importance and often exceed primary bone sarcoma in likelihood.

3 · Read the radiograph systematically

Bone destruction: geographic = discrete zone of loss, often a slower process; moth-eaten = irregular multiple defects; permeative = widespread tiny defects, suggesting aggressive growth. These are patterns, not standalone histologic diagnoses.

Periosteal reaction: a relatively contained, sclerotic response suggests slow growth. Aggressive lesions can elevate periosteum into a Codman triangle, radiate outward in a sunburst pattern, or form layered onion-skin periosteal new bone.

Matrix: osteoid/bone = amorphous or cloud-like ossification; cartilage = stippled, popcorn, or arcs-and-rings calcification; fibrous tissue = ground-glass appearance; some tumors have no mineralized matrix.

EXAM TRAP
A periosteal pattern is a clue to growth behavior, not an absolutely specific diagnosis. Combine it with age, region, matrix, and clinical presentation.
A painful aggressive metaphyseal mass near the knee has sunburst periosteal new bone and irregular osteoid matrix. Name the most likely tumor and explain why.
Osteosarcoma. A metaphyseal tumor in a young patient that makes bone and lifts periosteum is a classic osteogenic malignant pattern.

4 · Histology: benign versus malignant

At low power evaluate cellularity, architecture, circumscription, cortical permeation, soft tissue extension, necrosis and hemorrhage. At high power evaluate cytologic anaplasia, pleomorphism and mitoses. Malignant tumors may create matrix directly through malignant cells; this is critical in osteosarcoma.

MUST KNOW
The definitive morphologic distinction for osteosarcoma is malignant tumor cells directly producing osteoid, not simply finding reactive bone near a malignant tumor.

5 · Osteogenic tumors: osteoid osteoma & osteosarcoma

Osteoid osteoma: benign osteoblast neoplasm, usually age 10–30, male predominance, cortical diaphysis of femur/tibia; small radiolucent nidus under 2 cm with surrounding reactive sclerosis. Nocturnal pain is disproportionate to lesion size and responds dramatically to aspirin/NSAIDs because prostaglandin synthesis drives pain. Management includes NSAIDs or radiofrequency ablation; excellent prognosis.

Microscopy: small well-circumscribed nidus of irregular immature osteoid trabeculae rimmed by plump benign osteoblasts. Differentiate osteoblastoma (>2 cm in lecture) and osteomyelitis/abscess (inflammation).

FIRST AID CONNECTION
First Aid 2025 (printed p. 470) adds the explicit prostaglandin mechanism and emphasizes osteoblastoma as a size/pain-response differential. The course uses <2 cm for osteoid osteoma; First Aid quotes <1.5 cm. Preserve the lecture cutoff for the in-house exam.

Primary osteosarcoma: malignant mesenchymal tumor directly producing immature osteoid, often teenagers and young adults, with a second older-adult peak in secondary disease. Classically centered in the metaphysis around the knee (distal femur/proximal tibia) or proximal humerus; pain, enlarging tender mass and occasional pathologic fracture.

Imaging is intramedullary, mixed destructive/osteoblastic, with cortical breach, extension into soft tissue, sunburst and Codman triangle. Histology: malignant pleomorphic spindle cells, abnormal mitoses and lace-like osteoid, often high grade. Spread is hematogenous, predominantly to lungs; skip lesions may occur in the same bone.

Course treatment: neoadjuvant chemotherapy followed by wide surgery (limb salvage or amputation). Lecture links chemotherapy-induced necrosis with prognosis and highlights pulmonary metastasis. Genetic associations: RB1, TP53/Li-Fraumeni, radiation exposure or alkylating therapy. Secondary osteosarcoma follows Paget disease, fibrous dysplasia, retinoblastoma, radiation, or infarct, usually over age 50, with worse outcome.

LECTURE → STEP 1 BRIDGE
Adolescent + painful metaphyseal mass → malignant osteoid → sunburst/Codman triangle → recognize osteosarcoma; RB/TP53 susceptibility explains the board association.
Which histologic feature establishes osteosarcoma over an undifferentiated spindle-cell sarcoma with reactive bone?
Osteoid deposited directly by malignant cells.

6 · Chondrogenic tumors

Osteochondroma (exostosis): the lecture’s most common benign bone tumor. Usually 10–30 years, bony exophytic metaphyseal projection from an endochondral long bone with an orderly cartilage cap, and continuity of cortex and marrow with native bone. Often painless/incidental. Cap usually <2 cm, management observation or excision.

The lecture associates EXT1/EXT2 mutations with impaired chondrocyte differentiation; germline variants produce multiple hereditary exostoses with greater malignant transformation risk. Its slides quote both <1% and 1–5% for solitary transformation; these are differing lecture estimates, not a single precise risk.

Enchondroma (lecture: for familiarity only) is an intramedullary benign cartilaginous nodule, classically in hands/feet, often incidental, central/symmetric and lytic with focal calcification. Cartilage appears as bland chondrocytes in lacunae. Lecture associates IDH1/IDH2 changes with altered DNA methylation.

Chondrosarcoma: malignant cartilage-producing tumor, usually age 40–70, especially pelvis, proximal femur or humerus. Painful enlarging lesion with osteolysis, popcorn calcification, cortical destruction and soft-tissue extension; lecture notes no periosteal reaction as characteristic. Treatment is surgery.

Gross: large lobulated glistening blue-gray cartilage-like mass. Histology: malignant neoplastic cartilage infiltrating pre-existing bone, graded by cellularity, atypia and mitoses. Higher grade predicts greater recurrence/metastasis. IDH is linked to enchondroma-derived tumors and EXT to osteochondroma-derived tumors in the lecture.

COMMON CONFUSION
Osteochondroma protrudes outward, retains marrow continuity, and has a cartilage cap. Enchondroma sits inside marrow, often in small hand bones. Chondrosarcoma destroys/infiltrates native bone and may extend to soft tissue.
Why does a growing painful cartilage-capped exostosis in an adult deserve more attention than a stable incidental projection in a teenager?
A thickening cap, pain, growth after skeletal maturity or atypical/infiltrative cartilage can suggest secondary chondrosarcoma.

7 · Fibrous dysplasia

Fibrous dysplasia is a benign fibro-osseous lesion described in the lecture as maturation arrest: normal lamellar bone is replaced by irregular immature woven bone in fibroblastic stroma. The course associates somatic activating GNAS1 mutations with disruption of osteoblastic differentiation.

Forms: monostotic (70% in course; often incidental) and polyostotic (27% without endocrine syndrome; 3% with McCune–Albright). Earlier embryonic mutation causes wider distribution. McCune–Albright triad: polyostotic fibrous dysplasia, café-au-lait macules, and precocious puberty; other endocrine abnormalities may occur.

Imaging: expansile intramedullary ground-glass lesion, usually diaphysis/metaphysis, with possible proximal femoral varus deformity termed shepherd’s crook. Microscopy: irregular curving woven bone in proliferative fibrous stroma, without normal osteoblastic rimming as emphasized in the lecture. Treatment prevents deformity and stabilizes fractures; bisphosphonates occasionally.

CLINICAL CONNECTION
Weaker, disorganized woven bone in fibrous stroma → repeated mechanical failure/fracture → progressive remodeling → deformity.
What links café-au-lait macules, precocious puberty, and bone deformities in one patient?
Early postzygotic GNAS1 gain-of-function mutation causing McCune–Albright syndrome with mosaic tissue involvement.

8 · Giant cell tumor of bone

A locally aggressive / intermediate osteoclastic giant cell-rich lesion, classically in adults aged 20–40 after physeal closure. Centers in the epiphysis with extension to metaphysis; distal femur/proximal tibia, distal radius, sacrum. Expansile eccentric purely osteolytic “soap-bubble” lesion with non-sclerotic border and no calcified tumor matrix.

Histology: neoplastic mononuclear stromal cells plus reactive multinucleated osteoclast-like giant cells; neither bone nor cartilage tumor matrix is produced. Course notes H3F3A G34W alteration and osteoclast proliferation. In the pathology differential consider brown tumor of hyperparathyroidism, aneurysmal bone cyst and giant-cell-rich osteosarcoma.

Locally destructive with recurrence risk; may rarely metastasize to lung despite otherwise benign histology. Management includes curettage/cement or resection, with medical options denosumab (RANKL inhibitor) or bisphosphonates.

FIRST AID CONNECTION
First Aid 2025 (printed p. 470) emphasizes that tumor stromal cells express RANKL and recruit osteoclast-like giant cells; this supplies the mechanism for osteolysis and explains denosumab targeting RANKL.
Why can a tumor made of bland mononuclear cells and reactive giant cells aggressively destroy bone?
RANKL-mediated osteoclast recruitment/activation leads to extensive resorption despite the lack of overt malignant cytology.

9 · Ewing sarcoma

The lecture’s second most common pediatric malignant bone tumor, usually ages 10–20. A malignant small-round-cell neoplasm frequently centered in the diaphysis of long bones or pelvis. Pain, swelling, warmth, fever, leukocytosis and ESR elevation can mimic osteomyelitis.

Radiographs: poorly defined moth-eaten/permeative lytic diaphyseal lesion, layered onion-skin periosteal reaction, large non-mineralized soft tissue component; no osteoid matrix. Histology: sheets of uniform malignant small round blue cells, scant glycogen-rich cytoplasm; necrosis/mitoses.

Tumor genetics: t(11;22) → EWSR1–FLI1 fusion, the classic molecular association. Course mentions diffuse CD99 and additional immunostains; diagnosis relies on integrated pathology/molecular studies. Treatment multimodal: systemic chemotherapy with surgery ± radiation. Metastatic disease at diagnosis markedly worsens outlook.

FIRST AID CONNECTION
First Aid 2025 (printed p. 471): Ewing is in the small-round-blue-cell differential with lymphoma and osteomyelitis; t(11;22) / EWSR1–FLI1 helps distinguish its identity, while Ewing itself does not produce malignant osteoid.
A febrile 13-year-old has diaphyseal pain, onion-skin periosteal reaction, and a round-blue-cell biopsy. Which molecular change supports the tumor diagnosis?
EWSR1–FLI1 fusion due to t(11;22), supporting Ewing sarcoma.

10 · Metastases, synthesis & exam strategy

For an aggressive lesion in an older adult, metastatic carcinoma is the leading possibility before rare primary bone sarcoma. The lecture highlights breast, prostate, lung, kidney, thyroid and also hematopoietic tumors. Axial skeleton (spine, pelvis, ribs) is commonly involved. Prostate metastases are classically osteoblastic; many others are lytic or mixed.

BOARD / CLINICAL ENRICHMENT
When a lesion appears potentially malignant, tissue sampling should be planned with the treating orthopedic oncology team, because biopsy tract placement affects definitive resection. This is an additional clinical-practice principle, not a statement from the lecture.

Master these before moving on

Location is a diagnostic test

Before memorizing names, identify epiphysis/metaphysis/diaphysis and whether the growth plate has closed; this separates giant cell tumor, osteosarcoma, and Ewing.

Matrix reveals tumor differentiation

Bone-producing tumors make osteoid, cartilage-forming tumors calcify in arcs/rings/popcorn patterns, and fibrous dysplasia shows ground glass.

Histology answers who made the matrix

Osteosarcoma requires malignant cells producing osteoid. Reactive osteoblasts surrounding a lesion are not the same finding.

Aggressive radiology is not diagnosis alone

Use destructive pattern and periosteal reaction with patient age and histology rather than treating sunburst or onion skin as absolute identifiers.

Stromal cell signaling explains giant cell tumor

Neoplastic stromal cells recruit giant osteoclast-like cells; this creates osteolysis and explains RANKL blockade.

The most useful First Aid connections

  • Osteoid osteoma: prostaglandin-mediated nocturnal pain → NSAID relief; differentiate larger osteoblastoma.
  • Osteosarcoma: malignant osteoid + RB1/TP53 susceptibility + Codman triangle/sunburst.
  • Osteochondroma: EXT1/EXT2; cartilage-capped bony projection continuous with marrow and pointing away from a joint.
  • Giant cell tumor: tumor stromal RANKL recruits osteoclast-like giant cells; denosumab targets RANKL.
  • Ewing sarcoma: round blue cells + onion-skin diaphyseal lesion + t(11;22) EWSR1–FLI1.
